body:
What Is Gravitation?

A fruit falling from a tree, rain falling towards the ground, the Moon moving around Earth and planets revolving around the Sun appear to be different phenomena. However, all involve the same fundamental force: gravitation.

Gravitation is the force of attraction that exists between any 2 objects having mass.

Every object in the universe attracts every other object. This attraction exists between small objects, such as 2 books, as well as enormous bodies, such as Earth and the Sun. Gravitational attraction between ordinary objects is extremely weak, so we generally do not notice it. The gravitational attraction of Earth is easily observed because Earth has an enormous mass.

The gravitational force exerted by Earth on an object is commonly called gravity. Gravity is a non-contact force: Earth attracts objects without needing to touch them.

Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation

Sir Isaac Newton formulated the universal law of gravitation. According to this law, every object attracts every other object with a force that:

  • Is directly proportional to the product of their masses.
  • Is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
  • Acts along the line joining their centres.

For 2 objects of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), separated by a distance \(r\), the magnitude of gravitational force is:

$$F=G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$$

Here, \(F\) represents gravitational force, \(G\) is the universal gravitational constant, and \(r\) is the distance between the centres of the objects. The formula directly applies to point masses and to suitable spherically symmetric bodies when their centres are used.

Effect of Changing Mass

If the distance remains unchanged, gravitational force changes in direct proportion to the product of the masses. Doubling either mass doubles the force. Doubling both masses makes the force 4 times as large. Halving one mass reduces the force to half its original value.

Effect of Changing Distance

Gravitational force follows an inverse-square relationship. When the distance between the centres changes, the force changes according to the square of that distance.

  • If the distance doubles, the gravitational force becomes \(\frac{1}{4}\) of its original value.
  • If the distance triples, the force becomes \(\frac{1}{9}\) of its original value.
  • If the distance becomes half, the force becomes 4 times its original value.

These comparisons assume that the masses remain unchanged.

The Universal Gravitational Constant

The symbol G represents the universal gravitational constant. Its approximate value for school-level calculations is:

$$G\approx6.67\times10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}$$

The small numerical value explains why gravitational attraction between ordinary objects is difficult to notice. The recommended value in the 2022 CODATA adjustment is \(6.67430\times10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}\). This recommendation, released through the NIST database in May 2024, remained the latest published CODATA recommendation at the 3 November 2026 content cutoff. It uses measurement information available through 31 December 2022.

Henry Cavendish's experiments provided an important experimental determination of gravitational attraction, from which the value of G could be obtained.

Gravitational Attraction Is Mutual

When Earth attracts an apple, the apple also attracts Earth. The 2 gravitational forces have equal magnitude and opposite directions, consistent with Newton's third law of motion.

Earth does not noticeably move towards the apple because Earth's mass is enormously greater. According to Newton's second law, \(a=F/m\), so the same force produces much smaller acceleration in a much more massive object.

The gravitational forces acting on 2 interacting bodies are equal in magnitude, but their accelerations are generally unequal. Equal force does not mean equal acceleration.

Why the Universal Law Is Important

Newton's law provides a common explanation for several natural phenomena:

  • Falling objects: Earth attracts objects towards its centre.
  • The Moon's orbit: Earth's gravitational attraction continuously changes the Moon's direction of motion and provides the force needed to keep it in orbit.
  • Planetary motion: Gravitational attraction between the Sun and planets plays the central role in their orbital motion.
  • Ocean tides: The gravitational influences of the Moon and the Sun contribute to periodic changes in sea level.

The law is called universal because it applies to objects on Earth and to celestial bodies throughout the universe within the usual Newtonian description.

Prelims focus

  • Newton formulated the universal law of gravitation.
  • Gravitation is always attractive and is a non-contact force.
  • Gravitational force is directly proportional to the product of the masses.
  • Gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the centres.
  • The SI unit of G is N m2 kg-2.
  • Trap: Earth and an apple exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other, although their accelerations are very different.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, sections 10.1-10.1.2, printed pp. 131-134; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, Gravitation, section 9.1, printed pp. 100-102; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Fundamental Physical Constants Database, Newtonian Constant of Gravitation, 2022 CODATA recommendation, database updated May 2024, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Universal Gravitation: The Force of Attraction Between All Objects

body:
What Is Acceleration Due to Gravity?

When an object falls towards Earth under the influence of gravity, its velocity changes. This change in velocity occurs because Earth's gravitational force produces acceleration.

Acceleration due to gravity is the acceleration produced in an object by the gravitational attraction of Earth. It is represented by the small letter g.

Near Earth's surface, the commonly used approximate value is:

$$g\approx9.8\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$$

For simple calculations, the value may be rounded to \(10\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) when the question permits it.

The unit of g is metre per second squared because g represents acceleration. Near Earth's surface, its direction is approximately vertically downward, towards Earth's centre.

How g Is Related to Earth's Mass and Radius

According to the universal law of gravitation, the force acting on an object of mass \(m\) near Earth's surface is:

$$F=G\frac{Mm}{R^2}$$

Here, \(M\) represents Earth's mass and \(R\) its radius.

Newton's second law gives \(F=ma\). For acceleration produced by gravity, \(a=g\), so:

$$mg=G\frac{Mm}{R^2}$$

Dividing both sides by \(m\) gives:

$$g=\frac{GM}{R^2}$$

This relationship shows that surface gravitational acceleration depends on Earth's mass and radius, not on the mass of the falling object.

Consequently, a stone of mass 1 kg and another of mass 5 kg experience practically the same acceleration due to gravity when released at the same place, provided air resistance can be neglected. The heavier stone experiences greater gravitational force, but it also has proportionally greater mass.

Difference Between G and g

FeatureGg
MeaningUniversal gravitational constantAcceleration due to gravity
Approximate value6.67 × 10-119.8 near Earth's surface
SI unitN m2 kg-2m s-2
VariationUniversal constantChanges with location
DependenceDoes not depend on the particular interacting bodiesDepends on the attracting body's mass and the observation point

Why Does g Vary From Place to Place?

The approximate value of 9.8 m s-2 is useful for ordinary calculations, but Earth's gravitational acceleration is not exactly identical everywhere.

Variation With Height Above Earth's Surface

As an object moves away from Earth, the distance between the object and Earth's centre increases. Consequently, Earth's gravitational attraction and the resulting acceleration decrease.

Therefore, the value of g generally decreases with increasing altitude. A body taken to a sufficiently great height has a smaller weight than at Earth's surface, although its mass remains unchanged.

Variation From the Equator to the Poles

Earth is not a perfect sphere. It is slightly flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator. Consequently, the distance from Earth's centre to its surface is smaller at the poles than at the equator.

Earth's rotation also reduces the effective gravitational acceleration measured at the equator more than at the poles. These 2 effects make the effective value of g generally greater at the poles than at the equator.

At comparable elevations, g is greater at the poles and smaller at the equator.

Variation Below Earth's Surface

Below Earth's surface, the gravitational effect depends on how Earth's mass is distributed. In the simplified school model of a uniformly dense spherical Earth, g decreases as depth increases and becomes zero at the centre because the surrounding mass attracts equally in all directions.

Actual Earth does not have uniform density. Therefore, the simple statement that g decreases steadily with depth is a model-based approximation rather than an exact description of every depth within Earth.

Why g Is Treated as Constant in Simple Questions

The height of a classroom, building or small hill is extremely small compared with Earth's radius. Therefore, the corresponding change in g is generally negligible for elementary calculations.

This is why basic questions on falling objects commonly use a constant value of 9.8 m s-2 or 10 m s-2, even though g varies slightly from place to place.

Prelims focus

  • Acceleration due to gravity is represented by g.
  • The approximate value of g near Earth's surface is 9.8 m s-2.
  • Near Earth's surface, \(g=GM/R^2\).
  • g decreases as altitude increases.
  • Effective g is generally greater at the poles than at the equator.
  • Trap: G is the universal gravitational constant, whereas g is an acceleration that changes with location.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, sections 10.2-10.2.1, printed pp. 134-135; NASA Glenn Research Center, Weight Equation, section Altitude and Weight, consulted 3 November 2026; NOAA, The Downs and Ups of Gravity Surveys, discussion of Earth's rotation, shape and latitude, consulted 3 November 2026; IIT Kanpur SATHEE, Gravitation notes, section Variation of g with Depth, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Acceleration Due to Gravity: Meaning, Value and Variation

body:
Meaning of Free Fall

When a ball is released from a height, it starts moving downward because Earth attracts it. Its speed increases as it falls, provided the effects of air resistance are negligible.

An object is in free fall when gravity is the only force acting on it. Near Earth's surface, its acceleration is approximately g, directed downward.

Free fall does not require the object to be moving downward at every instant. A ball thrown vertically upward is also in free fall after it leaves the hand, if air resistance is neglected. Gravity acts throughout its upward journey, at the highest point and during its downward journey.

Free Fall of Heavy and Light Objects

Consider 2 objects of different masses released from the same height. In an ideal situation without air resistance, both objects accelerate downward at the same rate.

The gravitational force on a heavier object is greater. However, its greater mass means that proportionally greater force is required to produce the same acceleration. These 2 effects balance, so the acceleration is independent of the object's mass.

Thus, a heavy stone and a light stone released together from the same height reach the ground at the same time in a vacuum, provided they start with the same velocity.

Why a Flat Sheet of Paper Falls Slowly

A flat sheet of paper often falls more slowly than a compact stone. This difference arises mainly because the paper experiences substantial air resistance relative to its weight.

Crumpling the paper into a compact ball reduces the effect of air resistance, so it generally falls faster than the flat sheet. In the absence of air resistance, both forms fall with the same gravitational acceleration.

The statement that all objects fall at the same rate applies when air resistance and other forces are negligible. It does not mean that every object falls at the same speed under ordinary atmospheric conditions.

What Happens When a Ball Is Thrown Vertically Upward?

When a ball is thrown upward, its initial velocity is directed upward, but gravitational acceleration is directed downward. Gravity therefore reduces the upward velocity until the ball reaches its highest point.

At the highest point, the ball's instantaneous velocity becomes zero. However, its acceleration remains approximately 9.8 m s-2 downward.

After the highest point, the ball moves downward and its speed increases because both its motion and gravitational acceleration are downward.

Equations of Motion Under Gravity

For motion close to Earth's surface with negligible air resistance, the equations of uniformly accelerated motion can be used:

$$v=u+at$$

$$s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2$$

$$v^2=u^2+2as$$

Here, \(u\) is initial velocity, \(v\) is final velocity, \(a\) is acceleration, \(t\) is time and \(s\) is displacement along the chosen direction.

The sign of acceleration depends on the positive direction selected. If upward is positive, \(a=-g\). If downward is positive, \(a=+g\).

Simple Example: A Ball Dropped From Rest

Suppose a ball is dropped from rest and falls freely for 2 seconds. Take g = 9.8 m s-2 and downward as positive.

The initial velocity is zero, so:

$$v=0+9.8\times2=19.6\;\mathrm{m/s}$$

The distance fallen is:

$$s=\frac{1}{2}\times9.8\times2^2=19.6\;\mathrm{m}$$

Therefore, after 2 seconds, the ball has moved 19.6 m downward and has a downward speed of 19.6 m/s, neglecting air resistance.

Free Fall and Weightlessness

An object in free fall continues to experience gravitational attraction. However, if the object and its supporting surroundings fall together, the object may exert no supporting force and appear weightless.

Therefore, apparent weightlessness does not necessarily mean that gravity has disappeared. The distinction is between gravitational force and the force exerted by a support.

Prelims focus

  • Free fall means motion under gravity alone.
  • All objects have the same free-fall acceleration at a given location when air resistance is negligible.
  • The approximate direction of g near Earth's surface is downward.
  • At the highest point of vertical upward motion, velocity is zero but acceleration is not zero.
  • Air resistance explains why a flat paper sheet may fall more slowly than a compact stone.
  • Trap: An object moving upward after being thrown can still be in free fall.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 10, Gravitation, sections 10.2 and 10.2.2, printed pp. 134-136; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, Motion, equations of uniformly accelerated motion; NASA Glenn Research Center, Weight Equation, explanation of orbital free fall and apparent weightlessness, consulted 3 November 2026.]
